findings.why: At ~97 characters plus the ' | Gluten-Free Korea' suffix appended by layout.js, the title is roughly double the SERP truncation point, so the differentiating phrase 'Easy to Make at Home' will never render. The description is likewise ~178 characters and will be cut mid-sentence.
findings.fix: Cut the title to something like 'Is Tteok Gluten-Free? Butter Tteok, Explained' and trim the description to ~150 chars, e.g. 'Butter tteok is built on glutinous rice flour — no gluten. What's safe, what isn't, and how we make it at home for a fraction of cafe prices.'

findings.quote: As of recently, **E-Mart's No Brand line and various online grocery malls sell a pre-mixed blend of glutinous rice flour and tapioca starch.**
findings.why: The article carries zero external citations. Claims a reader would want to act on — the pre-mix product, shared-facility milling risk, the composition of glutinous rice flour — rest entirely on the author's say-so, which caps E-E-A-T authoritativeness for a health-adjacent query.
findings.fix: Link the actual No Brand product page with the date checked, and cite one primary source (e.g. a coeliac association or a national food-labelling authority page, with its publication date) for the 'glutinous rice contains no gluten' and shared-facility points.

criteria.evidence_quote: why rice cake is safe but tteokbokki isn't

criteria.note: The reader is given concrete, independent checks: ask the cafe about recipe and kitchen, look for the shared-facility statement on the bag (with the Korean phrase to look for), or control every input at home.

findings.quote: Plain rice cake, and simple desserts like butter tteok, are naturally gluten-free.
findings.why: This is an unhedged absolute in an FAQ that celiac readers will read as a standalone answer. It contradicts the article's own body, which correctly insists a gluten-free recipe is not a gluten-free finished product, and it extends the guarantee to 'plain rice cake' generally — a category that includes wheat-based and wheat-dusted product.
findings.fix: Rewrite as a bounded statement: 'Rice-flour tteok contains no gluten, but not all tteok is pure rice — some is made with wheat flour or wheat starch, and plain rice cake is often dusted or handled on shared surfaces. Confirm the flour and the kitchen before treating any tteok as celiac-safe.'

findings.quote: why rice cake is safe but tteokbokki isn't
findings.why: In Korea a large share of tteokbokki tteok is 밀떡 — made with wheat flour — so the rice cake itself is frequently the gluten source, not just the sauce. A celiac reader told the danger lies in what is 'added around it' could reasonably eat wheat tteok believing the cake is inherently safe.
findings.fix: Name 밀떡 explicitly wherever tteok is described as rice-based, and correct the framing to: the tteok may be 쌀떡 or 밀떡, so the cake itself must be verified alongside the sauce.

findings.quote: E-Mart's No Brand line and various online grocery malls sell a pre-mixed blend of glutinous rice flour and tapioca starch.
findings.why: A named retail line and product format presented with no product name, no link, and no date of checking. Readers are directed to buy it, so if the line, the blend, or its composition does not exist as described, the article has sent a celiac reader shopping for a phantom product — and 'various online grocery malls' is unfalsifiable padding.
findings.fix: Give the exact product name in Korean, the retailer page or a photo of the bag, and the date you saw it on shelf; drop the 'various online grocery malls' clause or name one.

findings.why: Korean grocery lines and flour blends are reformulated and discontinued without notice, and the piece gives no date for when this was true, so the claim cannot be aged by the reader.
findings.fix: Replace with an explicit check date ('confirmed on shelf, July 2026') and add a line telling readers to re-check the current bag's ingredient and allergen panel rather than relying on the article.
